To reduce something means to make it smaller, fewer, less, or lower than it was before. Think of it as pulling something down from its current level — shrinking it, cutting it, or bringing it to a lesser state.

There is always a before and an after with this word. Something existed at a certain level, and now it is lower, smaller, or less. That downward movement is what "reduce" is always about.
Everyday Uses

You can reduce almost anything that can be measured or felt — an amount, a size, a level, a cost, a degree of something.

  • The shop reduced its prices. → The prices went down.
  • She reduced her speed near the school. → She drove slower.
  • He reduced his sugar intake. → He ate less sugar.
  • The company reduced its workforce. → Fewer people were employed.
  • Regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease. → The risk becomes lower.

In all these cases, something that was at a certain level has been brought to a lower one. The word is factual and precise here — it doesn't carry strong emotion. It simply tells you: something went down.
"Reduce to" — The Most Powerful Pattern

One of the most important ways "reduce" works is with the word "to": reduce something to something. This describes transforming something into a far worse, simpler, or more broken state.

  • The fire reduced the house to ashes. → Nothing was left but ash.
  • The earthquake reduced the city to rubble. → The city was completely destroyed.
  • The cruel words reduced her to tears. → She broke down crying.
  • Centuries of neglect reduced the palace to a ruin.

Notice the weight here. Something that was whole, standing, grand, or dignified has been brought down to its most broken, raw, or devastated form. The word "to" marks where it ended up after the damage.
"Be Reduced to Doing Something"

There is a closely related pattern: be reduced to doing something. This means a person is forced by difficult circumstances into doing something they would never normally choose to do — usually something humble, desperate, or undignified.

  • After losing everything, he was reduced to begging on the street.
  • The drought left farmers reduced to rationing a single bucket of water a day.
  • She was reduced to borrowing money from strangers.

The feeling is of a fall — life has pushed someone down into a state they didn't want and wouldn't have accepted under normal circumstances.
In Cooking

When you reduce a liquid — a sauce, a broth, a gravy — you heat it so that water evaporates and the liquid shrinks in volume. What remains is thicker and more concentrated in flavour.

  • Reduce the sauce over medium heat until it thickens.
  • Reduce the stock by half.

The logic is the same: less volume, more intensity.
In Mathematics

To reduce a fraction means to simplify it — to divide the top and bottom by their common factor so the fraction is written in its smallest form. The value stays the same; the numbers just become simpler.

  • 4/8 reduces to 1/2.
  • 9/12 reduces to 3/4.
In Chemistry and Science

In chemistry, to reduce a substance means to add electrons to it. In older, more practical terms, it meant removing oxygen from a substance. For example, iron ore is reduced in a blast furnace: oxygen is stripped away from it to produce pure metal. The underlying idea — stripping something away, making something more elemental or simpler — still fits the word's core spirit.
In Medicine and Surgery

In medicine, to reduce a fracture or a dislocation means to put a broken or displaced bone back into its correct position. A doctor might reduce a dislocated shoulder by manipulating it back into the joint. Here, "reduce" carries a slightly different flavour — restoring something to its proper original state — but the idea of bringing something back to a simpler, fundamental form is still present.
In Rank and Status

In formal and military contexts, to reduce someone means to lower their rank — essentially, to demote them.

  • The officer was reduced to the rank of private after the misconduct.
The Word's Tone and Feel

In practical everyday contexts — reduce costs, reduce risk, reduce weight — "reduce" sounds neutral, controlled, and precise. It is the language of planning, management, and measurement.

But in the "reduce to" pattern — reduce to tears, reduce to ashes, reduce to nothing — the word becomes heavier and more dramatic. It suggests something has been devastated, humbled, or destroyed.

Despite these different shades, the one constant is this: something that was more has become less. Something that was higher is now lower. Something that was whole is now broken or simplified. Whether you're talking about prices, fractions, sauces, bones, or broken cities — reduce always describes that same downward journey.
